topics.title: Reading: The Concept of Life Skills

sections.heading: Main ideas and key terms
bullets: Life skills are abilities for adaptive, positive behavior that help people meet everyday demands and challenges. They support responsible choices, wellbeing, self-reliance and constructive participation in a community.
Core skills in the reading include decision-making, problem-solving, critical thinking, self-awareness, assertiveness, communication and conflict resolution.

Personal skills help people form and maintain relationships and support networks. Home-management skills include practical knowledge such as budgeting, nutrition and hygiene. Self-reliance skills help people organize their lives and use resources.

A sense of belonging involves connection, safety, acceptance and contribution. It supports social relationships and confidence; belonging does not require agreeing with everyone or giving up honest communication.
Life skills are learned and depend on context. Their exact form can differ across cultures and situations, even when the broad aim of effective everyday action is shared.

sections.heading: Reading and vocabulary strategy
bullets: Before reading, use the title and lead questions to predict the topic. While reading, identify topic sentences, supporting explanations, examples and contrast words.
After reading, state the central idea in your own words and distinguish it from individual examples or supporting details.
Use context clues to infer unfamiliar vocabulary: look for definition, synonym, contrast, example or cause-and-effect signals nearby.
For reference questions, locate the noun or idea that a pronoun points back to and check agreement in number and meaning.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define life skills and name at least four component skills.
Distinguish personal, home-management and self-reliance skills with an example.
Explain how belonging connects to interpersonal wellbeing without equating it with conformity.

sections.heading: Active and passive voice
bullets: Active voice places the doer as subject: The researcher measured the sample. Passive voice makes the receiver or process the focus: The sample was measured (by the researcher).

Form the passive with the appropriate tense of be + past participle. Preserve the tense and aspect: writes → is written; wrote → was written; has written → has been written; will write → will be written.
Use passive voice when the actor is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when a report emphasizes procedure and results. Include a by-phrase when the agent matters.
Only transitive verbs with an object normally form a personal passive. Keep subject–verb agreement and do not omit necessary auxiliaries.
Avoid passive voice when it makes the sentence needlessly vague; academic writing can use both voices for clarity.

sections.heading: Speaking and writing skills
bullets: In a short oral report, introduce the topic, present points in a logical order, use transitions and conclude clearly. Listen actively and respond to the speaker’s main point.
A paragraph develops one controlling idea with a topic sentence, supporting explanation or examples, and a closing or linking sentence.
An essay conclusion should provide a satisfying close, synthesize the central idea or show its significance, and avoid introducing a major new argument.
For note-making, use headings, keywords, abbreviations and brief phrases; distinguish main ideas from examples and rewrite notes in your own words.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Change an active sentence to passive while preserving tense, meaning and agreement.
Explain when passive voice suits an experiment or academic report.
Outline a coherent report or essay ending without adding a new topic.

units.title: Unit 2 - Speculations about the Future of Science

sections.heading: Reading focus
paragraphs: The unit’s reading examines a community-oriented response to bilharzia (schistosomiasis) and connects scientific knowledge with local participation. In comprehension questions, separate the problem described, the intervention, the people involved and the evidence or outcome reported.

sections.heading: Reading skills and discussion
bullets: Identify the author’s central claim and trace how examples and details support it.
Distinguish fact stated in the passage from a prediction, opinion or inference.
Discuss how scientific research and community knowledge can work together while checking claims against evidence.
When discussing future science, use cautious language for predictions and explain the reasons or evidence behind them.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Summarize the reading’s main issue and response in a few connected sentences.
Identify supporting details and explain how they relate to the main idea.
State a future-oriented claim with an appropriate degree of certainty.

sections.heading: Ways to refer to the future
bullets: Will + base verb often expresses a prediction, spontaneous decision, promise or offer: I think the method will help.
Be going to + base verb commonly expresses an intention or a prediction based on present evidence: They are going to test the water.
Present continuous can express a definite arrangement: The team is meeting the community tomorrow.
Simple present can refer to a timetable or fixed schedule: The seminar begins at nine.
Future continuous (will be + -ing) emphasizes an action in progress at a future time; future perfect (will have + past participle) emphasizes completion before a future point.

Time clauses with when, after, before, until and as soon as commonly use present forms for future meaning: When the study ends, we will report the results—not ‘when the study will end’ in this clause.

sections.heading: Speaking and writing
bullets: In a discussion about scientific possibilities, distinguish established facts from hypotheses and forecasts.
Support a prediction with a reason and use hedging expressions such as may, might, is likely to or probably when certainty is limited.
Organize a short future-focused paragraph with the current situation, expected change, reasons and possible implications.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Choose will, going to, present continuous or simple present according to the context—not only because a sentence contains a future time word.
Correct future time clauses after when, before, after and until.
Rewrite an overconfident prediction using language that matches the evidence.

topics.title: Reading: Environmental Challenges - A River Runs Through It

sections.heading: Reading focus
paragraphs: The unit uses a reading about environmental challenges and a river to develop comprehension and discussion. Track the environmental issue, its causes, affected communities or ecosystems, and proposed responses; distinguish description of a problem from evidence about its cause.

sections.heading: Critical reading
bullets: Look for cause-and-effect links and note whether the passage supports them with observations or examples.
Identify reference words, transition markers and paragraph relationships to follow the argument.
Summarize without copying: retain the key issue and response while removing repeated examples and minor details.
In speaking tasks, build on a partner’s point, ask for clarification and disagree respectfully with reasons.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: State the passage’s main environmental concern and supporting details.
Explain one cause-and-effect relationship and cite the passage evidence in your own words.
Give a concise summary that preserves the central message.

sections.heading: Modal verbs
bullets: Modals are followed by a base verb without ‘to’ in most cases: can protect, should reduce, must act. Do not add -s to the main verb after a modal.

Can/could express ability or possibility; may/might express possibility or permission; must expresses strong obligation or deduction; have to expresses necessity; should/ought to express advice or expectation.
Must not (mustn’t) means prohibition; do not have to means lack of necessity. These meanings are not interchangeable.
For past ability or possibility use context-appropriate forms such as could, was able to, may have + past participle or might have + past participle.
Modals can express degrees of certainty: must be is a strong deduction; may/might be is less certain; cannot be expresses strong impossibility.

sections.heading: Environmental proposals and paragraph writing
bullets: Use should or ought to for recommendations, must or have to for strong requirements, and may/might/could for possible consequences.
A persuasive paragraph states a position, gives reasons and evidence, addresses a relevant concern and ends with a clear recommendation.
Use connectors such as because, therefore, however, for example and as a result to show relationships accurately.
Avoid unsupported generalizations. Specify who is responsible, what action is proposed and why it may help.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish prohibition from absence of obligation.
Select a modal that matches whether a sentence expresses ability, advice, permission, possibility or necessity.
Write an environmental recommendation with a clear claim and relevant support.

topics.title: Reading: A Local Pathway to Global Development

sections.heading: Reading focus
paragraphs: This unit considers how locally grounded knowledge and practices can contribute to development. Analyze the example in the passage: identify the local knowledge, the need it addresses, how it is transmitted or applied, and the conditions that affect its wider use.

sections.heading: Comprehension and discussion
bullets: Distinguish the author’s main claim from examples and supporting details.
Consider how local experience can complement other forms of knowledge while asking how evidence, community participation and context are handled.
Use discussion turns to explain, clarify, compare and respectfully challenge an idea.
When summarizing a process, preserve its sequence and causal relationships rather than listing disconnected facts.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Explain the relationship between local knowledge and development presented in the reading.
Identify evidence or examples that support the author’s view.
Give a balanced response that recognizes both potential contributions and contextual limits.

sections.heading: Direct and reported speech
bullets: Direct speech quotes a speaker’s exact words. Reported speech conveys the meaning without quotation marks: She said, ‘I am ready’ → She said (that) she was ready.
When the reporting verb is in the past, pronouns and time/place expressions may shift to fit the new viewpoint: today→that day, here→there, this→that, tomorrow→the next day.

Backshift commonly changes present to past, present perfect to past perfect, will to would, and can to could. Backshift is not always necessary for facts still true or when the reporting verb is present.
Use say + clause; use tell + object + clause (He told us that…). Questions use ask/wonder and statement word order: ‘Where do you live?’ → She asked where I lived.
Yes/no questions use if or whether. Reported commands and requests commonly use tell/ask + object + to-infinitive; negative commands use not to.

sections.heading: Writing and reporting
bullets: In a report, identify the source or speaker, preserve the original meaning and distinguish quotation from paraphrase.
A coherent written report uses an opening that establishes context, organized findings or points, transitions and a conclusion.
Check tense, pronoun reference and time expressions after changing direct speech to reported speech.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Change a statement, yes/no question and wh-question into reported speech.
Explain when backshift may be unnecessary.
Report a request using an appropriate reporting verb and infinitive form.

topics.title: Reading: Cultural Heritage - What Is It? Why Is It Important?

sections.heading: Reading focus
paragraphs: The unit’s reading examines cultural heritage and its importance. In revision, distinguish tangible heritage (physical places and objects) from intangible heritage (knowledge, expressions, practices and skills), and connect preservation with identity, memory, learning and community life as presented in the passage.

sections.heading: Comprehension and response
bullets: Identify definitions, examples, reasons and conclusions in the passage.
Separate the author’s central argument from supporting instances of heritage.
Discuss preservation by considering who values, maintains and interprets heritage and how it can be transmitted responsibly.
Use specific examples to support an opinion rather than relying on broad claims.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define cultural heritage and distinguish tangible and intangible examples.
Explain why heritage matters using reasons from the reading.
Write a short response that connects preservation to community and future generations.

sections.heading: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
bullets: A relative clause modifies a noun. Who usually refers to people, which to things, that to people or things in defining clauses, whose indicates possession, and where/when refer to place/time.
A defining (restrictive) clause identifies which person or thing is meant and has no commas: The site that we visited is protected.
A non-defining clause adds extra information and is separated by commas: Lalibela, which is in Ethiopia, is known for its rock-hewn churches. Do not use that in a non-defining clause.
A relative pronoun can be omitted in a defining clause when it is the object, but not when it is the subject: The artifact (that) researchers found…; The artifact that survived…
Prepositions can appear before the relative pronoun in formal style (the community in which it developed) or at the end in more informal style (the community it developed in).

sections.heading: Academic speaking and writing
bullets: Use relative clauses to combine related ideas and avoid repetitive short sentences, but ensure each clause clearly modifies the intended noun.
An informative paragraph or essay uses a focused topic, explanation and evidence, with transitions that guide the reader.
Revise for unity, coherence, accurate grammar, punctuation and appropriate word choice. Read aloud to detect awkward or ambiguous sentences.
In presentations, explain key terms, organize information logically and conclude by reinforcing the central message.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Choose the relative pronoun that matches the noun and its grammatical role.
Add commas for non-defining clauses and do not use ‘that’ in them.
Combine two sentences with a relative clause without changing the intended meaning.
Review the five unit themes alongside their grammar focus: voices, future forms, modals, reported speech and relative clauses.
